characters: Joyce: an 11-year-old girl in a school uniform with a bright green cap, reading a magazine.
Pelpuo: an 11-year-old boy in a school uniform, sceptical and funny.
Madam Tagoe: their class teacher, in a yellow dress, with a clipboard and a broom.
The street: a clean, tree-lined road with community members sweeping together on a Saturday morning (story picture).

narrationPlan.voice: Cheerful voice for Joyce; wry voice for Pelpuo; warm voice for Madam Tagoe
narrationPlan.pace: Upbeat and brisk, with a smile in the debate (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Upbeat community drums and clapping; a cheerful sweeping rhythm (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The pupils and teacher are invented. Rwanda’s umuganda and bag ban facts come from published reports.
The story shows both the praise and the criticism of umuganda and lets pupils choose a voluntary approach.
Ghana’s National Sanitation Day is mentioned only as having existed and as a proposed compulsory measure in 2015. Check current practice locally.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: umuganda institutionalised in 1995; last Saturday of every month; about three hours from about 8 a.m.; ages given as 16 to 65 (UNDP) or 18 to 65 (NPR); fines for non-participation (5,000 Rwandan francs per NPR); single-use plastic ban in 2008; criticism as forced labour; shopkeepers’ complaints.
Check the Ghana lines against a current source: monthly National Sanitation Day existed; a 2015 bill proposed making participation compulsory and penalties for littering.
Check that the story shows a voluntary, safe, adult-supervised club and that dangerous work is done by adults.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about community cleaning and civic choice. It teaches how another country built a habit of shared cleaning and invites learners to weigh rules against voluntary action.
learningGoals: Describe what umuganda is and what it achieves.
Compare rules and voluntary action and give reasons.
beforeReading: Ask: have you ever helped to clean your street or school with others? How did it feel?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to note down both sides of the umuganda argument.
afterReading: Plan a clean-up: date, place, jobs, safety, snacks, who does the dangerous work.
Write a short invitation to parents and neighbours.
discussion: Is it fair to fine people who do not join? Why or why not?
What makes people want to join a clean-up?
reflection: What would make you give up one Saturday morning each month?

mathsExtension.task: The class filled 61 bags. If each bag had about 18 sachets, about how many sachets is that?
Umuganda lasts three hours starting at 8 a.m. When does it end?

support: Give a planning chart with who, what, where and when.
stretch: Find another country with a monthly clean-up tradition.

culturalNotes: The pupils and teacher are invented. Rwanda’s umuganda and bag ban facts come from published reports.
The story shows both the praise and the criticism of umuganda and lets pupils choose a voluntary approach.
Ghana’s National Sanitation Day is mentioned only as having existed and as a proposed compulsory measure in 2015. Check current practice locally.
localiseThis: Use your local National Sanitation Day customs; invite assembly staff to explain; follow safety rules.

factCheck.claim: Rwanda institutionalised umuganda in 1995; people take part on the last Saturday of each month (ages given as 16 to 65); a ban on single-use plastic bags and bottles was introduced in 2008; Kigali is regarded as the cleanest city in Africa; households separate waste and private companies collect it.
factCheck.explanation: From a UNDP blog on Rwanda’s fight against plastic pollution.
factCheck.reference: UNDP Rwanda, “Umuganda: Rwanda’s audacity of hope to end plastic pollution”.

factCheck.claim: Umuganda is held on the last Saturday of each month for about three hours from about 8 a.m.; able-bodied people aged 18 to 65 are required to take part; non-participants can be fined 5,000 francs; critics call it forced labour; shopkeepers complain about lost business.
factCheck.explanation: From a National Public Radio report (2018). It gives the age range as 18 to 65, which differs from UNDP’s 16 to 65.
factCheck.reference: NPR, “How Rwanda tidied up its streets and the rest of the country too”.

factCheck.claim: A bill proposed making littering a crime with possible imprisonment and making monthly National Sanitation Day participation compulsory; Cabinet was considering it in April 2015; critics urged Parliament to reject it.
factCheck.explanation: From a MyJoyOnline report dated 20 April 2015. The report does not say whether the bill became law.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Cabinet considers bill proposing prison sentence for littering”.
